[Thinking]
**Creating NCLEX to-do list**

The user wants a structured to-do list for passing the NCLEX. I should include actionable items like a timeline, study resources, practice questions, content review, test-taking strategies, registration, schedules, and self-care tips. Tailoring durations for each phase, like 3 months, 6 weeks, or one week before test day, might be helpful. I'll recommend question banks like UWorld and Kaplan, and include strategies for passing while ensuring reminders about eligibility and scheduling. I'll keep everything concise yet comprehensive.
[/Thinking]

Below is a focused, practical to‑do list to guide your NCLEX prep. Use it as a checklist you can mark off day-by-day. Adjust timing based on how many weeks you have.

Before you start
- Confirm eligibility and licensure application status with your state board.
- Register and schedule your NCLEX with Pearson VUE (or waitlist if needed).
- Gather required ID documents and understand test center rules.

Create your plan (Day 1)
- Set your exam target date and count backward to make a study calendar.
- Decide weekly study hours (e.g., 15–30 hrs/week depending on time until exam).
- Choose one main question bank (UWorld, Kaplan, Saunders Qbank, or NCSBN Learning Extension) and one comprehensive review book (Saunders, Lippincott, or RNNotes).

Foundational phase (weeks 1–4)
- Do a baseline test: 75–150 practice questions to identify strengths and weaknesses.
- Review core content by system: med-surg (CV, resp, neuro, GI, renal/endocrine), maternal/newborn, pediatrics, mental health, pharmacology.
- Create or use quick reference sheets for: common meds (classes, side effects, safe doses), labs/values & interpretation, infusion rates, acid–base, electrolytes.

Daily / weekly routine
- Do 30–75 timed practice questions/day with review (explain both right and wrong answers).
- Focus study blocks on weak topics identified in baseline and Qbank performance.
- Practice alternate-format items: SATA, drag-and-drop, fill-in-the-blank, hot spots, and case studies.
- Weekly full-length or block simulation (75–265 questions or 2–4 hour timed blocks) to build stamina.

Higher-yield focus areas
- Prioritization, delegation, and infection control (frequent NCLEX themes).
- Pharmacology and med safety (antidotes, interactions, high‑risk meds).
- Pediatrics growth/development and dosage calcs.
- Lab values: know normal ranges and what to do for critical abnormalities.
- Management of care, safety, client education.

Question strategy
- Read the scenario, identify the priority problem, determine the desired outcome, then choose the intervention.
- Use the “ABC, Maslow, safety, acute before chronic, unstable before stable” prioritization order.
- For SATA: pick all that apply—eliminate clearly wrong options first.
- For calculations: practice until fast and accurate; show work quickly then verify.

Weekly self-assessment
- Take at least one self‑assessment exam (NBME-style or Qbank CAT) every 1–2 weeks.
- Track trends: aim for progressive improvement in percentiles and decreasing topic weak spots.
- Adjust study plan to focus on persistent weaknesses.

Last month
- Increase mixed practice questions and simulated CATs; limit new content.
- Final review: high-yield notes, meds, lab values, key procedures, delegation rules.
- Do at least two full-length practice tests under exam conditions.

Last week
- Taper heavy studying 48–72 hours before exam—focus on review sheets, not learning new topics.
- Practice 1–2 short timed blocks, light review of meds and critical labs.
- Prepare test day items: route to center, ID, dress in layers, snacks for after, rest.

Test day
- Eat a light meal beforehand, avoid heavy or new foods.
- Bring required ID and any confirmation documents.
- Arrive early; use breaks strategically (short walk, hydration, light snack).
- Read each question carefully; pace yourself; use the given breaks.
- If you think you failed based on feeling, don’t assume—results are determined by the CAT algorithm.

Self-care throughout
- Sleep 7–9 hours nightly, get short daily exercise, maintain healthy meals.
- Use stress relief techniques: deep breathing, brief walks, mindfulness.
- Take at least one full day off every week to prevent burnout.

After the test
- Know how/when results are released for your jurisdiction.
- If unsuccessful, request a diagnostic report (if available), analyze weak areas, and create a retake plan.

Resources to consider
- Qbanks: UWorld, Kaplan Qbank, Saunders Q&A, NCSBN Learning Extension
- Review books: Saunders Comprehensive Review, Lippincott’s NCLEX Review
- Official practice: NCSBN NCLEX practice questions/exams
- Apps: flashcards for labs, meds, and growth milestones

If you want, tell me:
- how many weeks you have until your exam and your strongest/weakest subjects, and I’ll make a tailored weekly schedule.
